levels.title: Open the storefront
levels.concept: First-match order, implicit deny, least privilege, stateful replies

paragraphs: A firewall checks each new connection against its rules from the top down. The first rule whose every field matches decides: allow or deny. No later rule is looked at.
A connection that matches no rule is denied. This is the implicit deny, and it means you only need to write rules for what must be allowed.
The firewall is stateful: once a connection is allowed, its replies are allowed automatically. Only the direction of the first packet needs a rule.
Least privilege means the narrowest rule that still does the job: one destination and one port, not "any".
briefing.workedExample: Example (different from your task): a mail server 203.0.113.25 must receive mail on TCP 25. The rule "Allow Internet to 203.0.113.25 on TCP 25" is enough. A request to 203.0.113.25 on TCP 80 matches no rule, so the implicit deny stops it. No deny rule was needed.
simplifications: This game models a firewall that checks rules in order and stops at the first match. Some real firewalls process rules differently.
Address translation and routing are not modeled; hosts are reached by the address shown.

standard.request: Customers on the Internet must reach the web server WEB-1 (203.0.113.10) on HTTPS, TCP 443. Nothing else may enter the DMZ from the Internet. WEB-1 does not need to start any connections of its own.

arcade.mission: LET IN 443 TO WEB-1. BLOCK EVERYTHING ELSE.

topology.description: Two zones separated by your firewall. The Internet zone holds customers and attackers. The DMZ zone holds the web server WEB-1 and a management host JUMP-1.

R1.label: Allow Internet to WEB-1 on TCP 443

R2.label: Allow Internet to the DMZ, anything

R3.label: Deny Internet to the DMZ, anything

R4.label: Allow Internet to WEB-1 on TCP 80 and 443

R5.label: Allow Internet to the DMZ on TCP 22

R6.label: Allow WEB-1 out to the Internet, anything
R6.note: so the web server can reply

R7.label: Allow Internet to WEB-1 on TCP 8080

requiredFlows.label: A customer opens the web site

attackSteps.label: Password guessing over SSH against JUMP-1
attackSteps.lesson: A remote-access service reachable from the Internet can be attacked by anyone on the Internet. Nothing in the request needed SSH from outside.

attackSteps.label: Exploit attempt against an admin console on WEB-1
attackSteps.lesson: Every extra port open on a public server is another application an attacker can try to exploit. Expose only the service that was requested.

attackSteps.label: Remote desktop connection to JUMP-1
attackSteps.lesson: Remote desktop should never be reachable from the Internet. Only a rule that allows far more than the request could have let this in.

probes.label: Plain HTTP to WEB-1 on TCP 80
probes.lesson: The request asked for HTTPS on TCP 443 only. Port 80 is extra exposure nobody asked for.

probes.label: WEB-1 starts a new connection out to the Internet
probes.lesson: Replies to customers are allowed automatically because the firewall is stateful. An outbound rule only lets a compromised server call out to an attacker.

rival.name: Rival firewall
rival.note: The rival opened SSH to the whole Internet "for vendor support".

hints: Method: for each thing the request says must work, find the narrowest rule that allows exactly that. Then ask what happens to everything else when no rule matches it.
Worked step: the request names one destination (203.0.113.10) and one port (TCP 443). Rule R1 matches exactly that and nothing more. Check whether you need any other rule at all.

paragraphs: You have inherited a nine-rule DMZ rule base. First match wins, unmatched traffic is denied, and replies need no rule.

Look for rules that are never reached, rules that repeat another rule, and rules wider than the request. A deny for one specific source only works if it sits above every allow that source could match.
briefing.workedExample: Example (different from your task): "Allow any to 203.0.113.40 on TCP 443" above "Deny 198.51.100.9 to anything" lets 198.51.100.9 reach the server, because the allow matches first and the deny is never reached.
simplifications: This game models a firewall that checks rules in order and stops at the first match. Some real firewalls process rules differently.
This level has no content inspection, so only a rule can stop the known-bad address.

expert.request: Customers reach WEB-1 (203.0.113.10) on TCP 443. Internet mail servers reach MAIL-1 (203.0.113.25) on TCP 25. Only the support partner (198.51.100.200) reaches JUMP-1 (203.0.113.20) on TCP 22. The known-bad address 198.51.100.66 reaches nothing. MAIL-1 may send mail out on TCP 25; no other DMZ host starts outbound connections.

orders.text: NEW ORDER: THE PARTNER NEEDS SSH (22) TO JUMP-1
NEW ORDER: MAIL (25) IN TO MAIL-1 AND OUT FROM MAIL-1

intro.text: Let customers in, keep attackers out

topology.description: Two zones separated by your firewall. The DMZ holds WEB-1, JUMP-1, and MAIL-1. The Internet holds a customer, a mail server, the support partner, one address already known to be hostile, and one attacker nobody has seen before.

E1.label: Allow Internet to WEB-1 on TCP 80 and 443

E2.label: Allow Internet to the DMZ on TCP 22

E3.label: Allow the support partner to JUMP-1 on TCP 22

E4.label: Deny the known-bad address to the DMZ, anything

E5.label: Allow Internet to MAIL-1 on TCP 25

E6.label: Allow Internet to WEB-1 on TCP 443

E7.label: Allow the DMZ out to the Internet, anything

E8.label: Allow MAIL-1 out to the Internet on TCP 25

E9.label: Allow Internet to WEB-1 on TCP 8080

requiredFlows.label: A customer opens the web site
An Internet mail server delivers mail to MAIL-1
The support partner connects to JUMP-1 over SSH

attackSteps.label: Password guessing over SSH against JUMP-1
attackSteps.lesson: SSH was meant for one partner address. A rule without a source lets every address on the Internet try passwords.

attackSteps.label: Exploit attempt against an admin console on WEB-1
attackSteps.lesson: The admin console was never in the request. Expose only the services that are meant to be public.

attackSteps.label: Exploit attempt from the known-bad address against the web site
attackSteps.lesson: A blocklist deny only works if it sits above every allow the blocked address could match. Below the web allow, it is never reached.

attackSteps.label: WEB-1 calls back out to the attacker
attackSteps.lesson: Restricting outbound traffic from public servers stops a compromised server from reaching its controller. Only MAIL-1 needed to start connections.

attackSteps.label: Remote desktop connection to JUMP-1
attackSteps.lesson: Remote desktop should never be reachable from the Internet.

probes.label: Plain HTTP to WEB-1 on TCP 80
probes.lesson: The request asked for TCP 443 only. A second rule already covers it without port 80.

probes.label: JUMP-1 starts a connection out to the Internet
probes.lesson: Only MAIL-1 may start outbound connections.

probes.label: The known-bad address connects to MAIL-1 on TCP 25
probes.lesson: The known-bad address must reach nothing, including the mail server. The blocklist has to sit above the mail allow too.

rival.name: Rival firewall
rival.note: The rival tidied up the allows but left the blocklist at the bottom, where it is never reached.

hints: Method: for each allow rule, ask whether the request needs it and whether a narrower rule already covers it. Then check that each deny sits above everything it is meant to override.
Worked step: E2 allows SSH from any source, so E3 (the partner-only rule) is never needed while E2 is there. Remove E2 and E3 starts doing the job.

levels.title: Let staff browse safely
levels.concept: Application identification, threat inspection, TLS decryption, DNS filtering

paragraphs: A port number does not tell you which application is using it. Many tools can run over TCP 443. A next-generation firewall can identify the application itself, so a rule can allow "HTTPS web browsing" and not just "TCP 443".
Allow rules can carry security controls. Threat inspection looks inside allowed traffic for malware and exploits. DNS filtering stops lookups of known-malicious domains.
Inspection can only work on content it can read. Web traffic is encrypted, so threat inspection needs TLS decryption switched on for the same rule. TLS decryption stops nothing by itself.
briefing.workedExample: Example (different from your task): a rule allows the "file transfer" application with threat inspection on. An unencrypted transfer carrying malware is stopped. The same transfer inside an encrypted session passes, because inspection cannot read it, until TLS decryption is switched on for that rule.
simplifications: The firewall in this game identifies every application and user correctly and at once. A real firewall may pass a few packets first.
The sources say these controls can mitigate an attack. The game simplifies that to "always stops".
Real decryption policies exempt some traffic, and some threats can be spotted without decryption. Neither is modeled. DNS over HTTPS is not modeled.

standard.request: Staff must be able to browse the web over HTTPS and resolve names through the approved DNS resolver (198.51.100.53). Malware downloads and command-and-control traffic must be stopped.

topology.description: Two zones separated by your firewall. The Users zone holds a staff workstation. The Internet holds the approved DNS resolver, ordinary web sites, an unapproved resolver, and an attacker-run server.

R1.label: Allow Users to the Internet on TCP 443 (by port)

R2.label: Allow Users to the Internet, application: HTTPS web browsing

R3.label: Allow Users to the approved resolver, application: DNS

R4.label: Allow Users to any destination on UDP 53

R5.label: Allow Users to the Internet, anything

requiredFlows.label: Staff browse a web site over HTTPS
Staff resolve a name through the approved resolver

attackSteps.label: A remote-access tunnel on the web port
attackSteps.lesson: TCP 443 is a port, not an application. A port-based rule allows anything that uses that port, including a tunnel out of the network.

attackSteps.label: A malware download over HTTPS
attackSteps.lesson: Threat inspection cannot read content that is still encrypted. It needs TLS decryption on the same rule to see the download.

attackSteps.label: A command-and-control lookup through DNS
attackSteps.lesson: Malware uses ordinary DNS lookups to find its controller. DNS filtering on the rule that allows DNS stops lookups of known-malicious domains.

probes.label: DNS to an unapproved resolver
probes.lesson: The request named one approved resolver. Allowing DNS to any destination lets a workstation use a resolver you do not control.

probes.label: Mail sent straight to the Internet on TCP 25
probes.lesson: Nothing in the request needed workstations to send mail directly.

rival.name: Rival firewall
rival.note: The rival allowed the web by port number and switched on inspection without decryption.

hints: Method: choose rules that name the application, not just the port. Then for each rule ask which control looks for the threat in the request, and whether that control can read the traffic.
Worked step: for web browsing, R2 names the application. Switch on threat inspection for it, then ask whether inspection can read HTTPS without TLS decryption.

paragraphs: You have inherited an eight-rule outbound rule base with controls already set, some of them wrongly. Rules can match on user group as well as application.
Check every allowed web flow: is it matched by application, is it inspected, and can the inspection read it? A destination you trust still needs all three.
briefing.workedExample: Example (different from your task): "Allow Finance to the payroll provider" with inspection off. If the provider is compromised, whatever it serves reaches Finance uninspected. Trust in the destination is not a control.
simplifications: The firewall in this game identifies every application and user correctly and at once. A real firewall may pass a few packets first.
The sources say these controls can mitigate an attack. The game simplifies that to "always stops".
Decryption exemptions and DNS over HTTPS are not modeled.

expert.request: Staff browse the web over HTTPS. Contractors reach only the vendor portal (198.51.100.150). Everyone resolves names only through the approved resolver (198.51.100.53). All allowed web traffic is decrypted and inspected, and DNS is filtered.

topology.description: Two zones separated by your firewall. The Users zone holds a staff workstation (group Staff) and a contractor workstation (group Contractors). The Internet holds the approved resolver, an ordinary web site, the vendor portal, an unapproved resolver, and an attacker-run server.

X1.label: Allow Users to the Internet on TCP 443 (by port)

X2.label: Allow Staff to the Internet, application: HTTPS web browsing

X3.label: Allow Contractors to the Internet, application: HTTPS web browsing

X4.label: Allow Contractors to the vendor portal, application: HTTPS web browsing

X5.label: Allow Users to any destination on UDP 53

X6.label: Allow Users to the approved resolver, application: DNS

X7.label: Allow Staff to 198.51.100.80, application: HTTPS web browsing

X8.label: Allow Users to the Internet, application: remote-access tunnel

requiredFlows.label: Staff browse a web site over HTTPS
A contractor opens the vendor portal
Staff resolve a name through the approved resolver
A contractor resolves a name through the approved resolver

attackSteps.label: A remote-access tunnel on the web port
attackSteps.lesson: Two different rules can let a tunnel out: one that matches the port, and one that names the tunnel application for everyone. Both are wider than the request.

attackSteps.label: A contractor downloads malware from an attacker site
attackSteps.lesson: Contractors were meant to reach one portal. A rule letting them browse anywhere, uninspected, lets them fetch anything.

attackSteps.label: Staff download malware over HTTPS
attackSteps.lesson: Threat inspection cannot read content that is still encrypted. It needs TLS decryption on the same rule.

attackSteps.label: A command-and-control lookup through DNS
attackSteps.lesson: DNS filtering has to be on for the rule that actually matches DNS traffic.

attackSteps.label: The compromised vendor portal serves malware to a contractor
attackSteps.lesson: A trusted destination still needs inspection. A partner site can be compromised, and an uninspected rule passes whatever it serves.

probes.label: DNS to an unapproved resolver
probes.lesson: Everyone was meant to use only the approved resolver.

probes.label: A contractor browses an ordinary web site
probes.lesson: Contractors were meant to reach only the vendor portal. Inspecting their general browsing does not make it requested.

rival.name: Rival firewall
rival.note: The rival narrowed every rule but left the vendor portal uninspected because it is "trusted".

hints: Method: work one request sentence at a time. Keep the single narrowest rule for it, remove the wider ones, then set that rule's controls so the traffic is both readable and inspected.
Worked step: X1 matches every TCP 443 connection before X2 is reached. Remove X1, then give X2 threat inspection and TLS decryption.

orders.text: LET STAFF BROWSE THE WEB AND USE DNS
NEW ORDER: CONTRACTORS NEED THE VENDOR SITE, NOTHING ELSE

intro.text: APP gates check what the traffic really is, not just its port
Flip a gate's switches to scan what it lets through
Locked traffic needs DECRYPT before SCAN can see inside

levels.title: Clean up the data center
levels.concept: User identity, segmentation, shadowed rules, lateral movement

paragraphs: Being inside the network does not make traffic trustworthy. A phished workstation or a compromised web server is already inside. Rules between internal zones decide how far an attacker can move.
A rule can match on user group, so access can follow who the user is and not just where they sit.
A rule is shadowed when a rule above it always matches first, so it is never reached. Removing the rule on top brings the shadowed rule back to life, whether it allows or denies.
An allowed application can still carry an exploit. Threat inspection on the allow rule looks for it.
briefing.workedExample: Example (different from your task): rule 1 "Allow Users to Servers, anything", rule 2 "Deny Users to the HR server". Rule 2 is shadowed. Remove rule 1 and rule 2 suddenly denies everyone, including the HR staff who relied on rule 1.
simplifications: This game models a firewall that checks rules in order and stops at the first match. Some real firewalls process rules differently.
The firewall in this game identifies every application and user correctly and at once. A real firewall may pass a few packets first.
The sources say these controls can mitigate an attack. The game simplifies that to "always stops".
Traffic in this level is unencrypted, so TLS decryption is not offered. The database port shown (TCP 5432) is illustrative.

standard.request: Only DB-Admins and the web server WEB-1 may reach DB-1 (10.20.0.10), and only with the database application. Nothing else may enter the Servers zone. All traffic into Servers must be inspected for threats.

topology.description: Three zones separated by your firewall. Users holds a database administrator (group DB-Admins) and a staff workstation (group Staff). The DMZ holds the public web server WEB-1. Servers holds the database DB-1 and an application server APP-2.

R3.label: Allow DB-Admins to DB-1, application: database

R4.label: Allow WEB-1 to DB-1, application: database

R5.label: Allow WEB-1 to Servers on TCP 22

requiredFlows.label: A database administrator works on DB-1

attackSteps.label: A phished staff workstation connects to the database
attackSteps.lesson: The workstation is inside the network, but its user is not a database administrator. A rule that allows the whole Users zone ignores who is asking.

attackSteps.label: The same workstation opens remote desktop to APP-2
attackSteps.lesson: Rules between internal zones are what stop an attacker moving from one machine to the next.

attackSteps.label: The compromised WEB-1 opens SSH to DB-1
attackSteps.lesson: WEB-1 needed the database application and nothing else. A leftover SSH rule gives a compromised web server a way into the servers.

attackSteps.label: The compromised WEB-1 sends an exploit inside its database session
attackSteps.lesson: This traffic has to be allowed, because the web site needs the database. Only inspecting the allowed session can stop an exploit carried inside it.

probes.label: WEB-1 opens SSH to APP-2
probes.lesson: WEB-1 was meant to reach DB-1 with the database application only.

probes.label: A database administrator opens a file share on APP-2
probes.lesson: DB-Admins were meant to reach DB-1 only.

probes.label: A database administrator's session carries an exploit
probes.lesson: The request said all traffic into Servers is inspected. An administrator's workstation can be compromised too.

rival.name: Rival firewall
rival.note: The rival cleaned up the rules perfectly but never switched on inspection.

hints: Method: for each rule, ask which request sentence needs it. Remove what nothing needs. Before removing a rule, check what the rules beneath it will start doing. Then check every remaining allow rule is inspected.

Worked step: R1 allows everything from Users, so R2 and R3 are never reached. If you remove only R1, R2 becomes the first match for the database administrators and denies them. R2 has to go too, or move below R3.

paragraphs: You have inherited an eight-rule data-center rule base with no inspection switched on. Rules match on zone, user group, address, port, and application.

Watch for rules that match a port where the request named an application, and for rules whose source is wider than the request. Inspection looks for malware and exploits; it does not turn the wrong application into the right one.
briefing.workedExample: Example (different from your task): "Allow Staff to the print server on TCP 9100" with inspection on. A remote-control tool using TCP 9100 matches the rule and carries nothing inspection would flag, so it passes. A rule naming the printing application would not have matched it.
simplifications: This game models a firewall that checks rules in order and stops at the first match. Some real firewalls process rules differently.
The firewall in this game identifies every application and user correctly and at once. A real firewall may pass a few packets first.
The sources say these controls can mitigate an attack. The game simplifies that to "always stops".
Traffic in this level is unencrypted. The database port shown (TCP 5432) is illustrative.

expert.request: DB-Admins and WEB-1 reach DB-1 (10.20.0.10) with the database application. Staff reach APP-2 (10.20.0.20) with the file-sharing application. Nothing else enters the Servers zone. All of it is inspected.

topology.description: Three zones separated by your firewall. Users holds a database administrator (group DB-Admins only) and a staff workstation (group Staff only). The DMZ holds WEB-1 and JUMP-1. Servers holds the database DB-1 and the file server APP-2.

Y3.label: Allow DB-Admins to DB-1, application: database

Y4.label: Allow Staff to APP-2 on TCP 445 (by port)

Y5.label: Allow Staff to APP-2, application: file sharing

Y6.label: Allow WEB-1 to DB-1, application: database

Y7.label: Allow the DMZ to DB-1, application: database

Y8.label: Allow WEB-1 to Servers on TCP 22

requiredFlows.label: A database administrator works on DB-1
Staff open a file share on APP-2

attackSteps.label: A phished staff workstation connects to the database
attackSteps.lesson: A rule that allows the whole Users zone ignores who is asking.

attackSteps.label: The same workstation opens remote desktop to APP-2
attackSteps.lesson: Staff needed file sharing on APP-2, not remote desktop.

attackSteps.label: Remote command execution over the file-sharing port
attackSteps.lesson: Inspection does not rescue a rule that allows the wrong application. This traffic carries nothing to flag; it is simply not file sharing, and a port-based rule cannot tell.

attackSteps.label: Malware copied to APP-2 through the file share
attackSteps.lesson: The right application can still carry malware. Threat inspection on the rule that allows file sharing stops the transfer.

attackSteps.label: The compromised JUMP-1 connects to the database
attackSteps.lesson: Only WEB-1 needed the database. A rule for the whole DMZ gives every other DMZ host the same access.

attackSteps.label: The compromised WEB-1 sends an exploit inside its database session
attackSteps.lesson: This traffic has to be allowed. Only inspecting the allowed session can stop an exploit carried inside it.

probes.label: WEB-1 opens SSH to APP-2
probes.lesson: WEB-1 was meant to reach DB-1 with the database application only.

probes.label: A database administrator's session carries an exploit
probes.lesson: The request said all traffic into Servers is inspected.

probes.label: A database administrator opens a file share on APP-2
probes.lesson: File sharing on APP-2 was for Staff, not DB-Admins.

rival.name: Rival firewall
rival.note: The rival kept the port-based file-sharing rule, which cannot tell file sharing from remote command execution.

hints: Method: match each request sentence to exactly one rule, the narrowest that names the application. Remove the rest, checking what each removal uncovers. Then switch on inspection for every allow rule that remains.
Worked step: Y4 and Y5 both let Staff reach APP-2 on the file-sharing port. Y4 matches the port, so it also matches anything else using TCP 445. Keep Y5 and remove Y4.

orders.text: LET DB-ADMINS AND WEB-1 REACH THE DATABASE
NEW ORDER: STAFF NEED THE FILE SHARE ON APP-2

intro.text: Gates can name who is allowed, not just where they go
A break-in elsewhere must not spread to your servers
Even trusted traffic can carry an exploit. Scan it.
